base_properties.human_readable: Organization Floor in Democratic Policy Markets

stakeholders.name: organized_labor_unions
stakeholders.situation: Maintain warrantable leadership structures, punishment mechanisms for defection, and delivery infrastructure that makes their members' preferences tradable in policy markets. They negotiate directly with legislators and executives, trading bloc votes for policy concessions. The organization floor is what makes this position possible — without it, their members' preferences would be as non-transactable as any other mass public's.

stakeholders.name: professional_associations
stakeholders.situation: Convert diffuse professional interests into tradable policy positions through credentialing bodies, lobbying arms, and member discipline. They capture regulatory rents by being the only organized voice in technical policy domains where mass publics have preferences but no transaction capacity.

stakeholders.name: industry_coalitions
stakeholders.situation: Pool resources across firms to clear the organization threshold, then trade concentrated industry positions against diffuse consumer or environmental interests that cannot organize at comparable scale. The floor protects them from being outbid by larger but unorganized populations.

stakeholders.name: political_party_machines
stakeholders.situation: Broker between organized blocs and policy outcomes. They set the terms of trade in the policy market and extract rents from the brokerage function itself. The organization floor is what creates the market structure they intermediate — without it, they would face direct preference aggregation rather than bloc negotiation.

stakeholders.name: unorganized_mass_publics
stakeholders.situation: Hold intense preferences on policy questions but cannot convert those preferences into tradable positions because they lack warrantable leadership, punishment capacity, or delivery infrastructure. Their preferences are systematically discounted in policy markets regardless of population size or intensity. Organizing is theoretically possible but faces prohibitive transaction costs.

stakeholders.name: diffuse_consumer_interests
stakeholders.situation: Bear concentrated costs from policies negotiated between organized producer blocs and political machines. Classic Olsonian structure: small per-capita costs, massive aggregate harm, no organization capacity because the per-capita benefit of organizing is below the participation cost.

stakeholders.name: geographically_dispersed_minorities
stakeholders.situation: Face systematic policy exclusion because their preferences cannot be geographically concentrated into tradable blocs. Electoral geography and the organization floor interact to make their positions non-transactable even when they would organize if the floor were lower.

stakeholders.name: political_scientists
stakeholders.situation: Study the organization floor as an empirical regularity in democratic systems. They debate whether it is a natural law of collective action or a constructed feature of specific institutional arrangements, and whether organized interests' systematic advantage is an efficiency property or a distributional pathology.

stakeholders.name: constitutional_reformers
stakeholders.situation: Propose institutional changes that would lower the organization floor — direct democracy mechanisms, sortition, quadratic voting, liquid representation. They are systematically excluded from policy markets because the organized blocs that benefit from the current floor control the reform agenda itself.

six_questions.coordination_function: Solves the warrantability problem in democratic policy exchange: legislators need credible commitments that bloc leaders can deliver votes, and voters need credible commitments that legislators will deliver policy. Organization provides the infrastructure for both.
six_questions.transfer_function: Transfers policy influence from unorganized mass publics to organized blocs. Policies systematically favor concentrated organized interests over diffuse unorganized ones, even when the latter are larger in population and more intense in preference.
six_questions.absent_voices: Constitutional reformers and direct democracy advocates who would lower the organization threshold are excluded from the reform conversation because organized blocs control the institutional change process itself. Unorganized publics are structurally absent from policy negotiation.
six_questions.disappearance_rationale: Political scientists dispute whether the organization floor would persist in the absence of specific institutional features (geographic representation, first-past-the-post voting, legislative procedure rules) or whether it is an irreducible property of any large-scale democratic system. Organized blocs claim it would persist as a natural law; reformers claim institutional changes would substantially lower it.
six_questions.founding_problem: Early democratic systems faced a warrantability crisis: how could legislators credibly commit to mass publics when individual voters had no punishment capacity, and how could voters credibly commit to legislators when individual votes were unverifiable? Organization solved this by creating intermediate structures with both punishment capacity and delivery infrastructure.
six_questions.founding_problem_corroboration: Organized blocs attest the warrantability problem is still live and organization is the only solution. Political scientists outside the benefiting blocs attest that modern communication technology and alternative voting mechanisms have substantially reduced the transaction costs that made organization necessary, and that the floor now persists partly through institutional inertia and partly through organized interests' active defense of the institutional features that maintain it.

commentary.narrative_context:
The organization floor in democratic policy markets describes a structural threshold below which mass preferences cannot be converted into tradable policy positions. The constraint appears as a natural law — an emergent property of transaction costs and collective action problems — but the presence of identifiable beneficiaries who systematically capture advantage from the floor's existence triggers false summit evaluation. The claim is Mountain (the constraint presents as a natural feature of democratic systems), while the metrics describe moderate extraction that has accumulated over time as organized interests have defended institutional features that maintain the floor against technological and institutional changes that would lower it.

KEY AGENTS (by structural relationship):
- Organized labor unions, professional associations, industry coalitions: Primary beneficiaries (organized/powerful, mobile/arbitrage exit) — systematic policy advantage from being above the floor
- Political party machines: Agenda setters (institutional, constrained exit) — broker the policy market the floor creates
- Unorganized mass publics, diffuse consumer interests, geographically dispersed minorities: Victims (powerless, trapped exit) — preferences systematically discounted
- Political scientists: Analytical observers — study the floor as empirical regularity
- Constitutional reformers: Excluded voices (moderate, constrained exit) — would lower the floor but are kept out of reform process
commentary.logic_rationale: Extraction is moderate (0.42) because the floor does solve a real coordination problem (warrantability in policy exchange) but the solution systematically advantages organized over unorganized interests beyond what transaction cost minimization would require. The measurement series shows accumulation over time as organized interests have defended institutional features that maintain the floor even as technology has reduced the underlying transaction costs. Suppression is moderate-low (0.38) because organizing is theoretically possible but faces prohibitive costs for most mass publics. Theater is low (0.22) because the coordination function is real, though a growing share of organized activity defends the floor itself rather than solving the warrantability problem. Accessibility collapse is high (0.78) because once you understand the organization threshold, the alternatives to organizing largely disappear — you either clear the floor or your preferences are non-transactable. Resistance is moderate-low (0.31) because most actors treat the floor as a natural law rather than a constructed feature, though constitutional reformers and some political scientists contest this.
commentary.directionality_logic: Organized blocs are structural beneficiaries — they sit above the floor and capture systematic policy advantage from its existence. Their directionality is near the beneficiary end. Unorganized mass publics are the targets — they sit below the floor and bear the extraction. Their directionality is near the target end, amplified by trapped exit options. Political party machines are agenda setters who extract rents from the brokerage function the floor creates — they benefit from the floor's existence but in a different way than the organized blocs. Political scientists are analytical observers with no structural position.
commentary.perspectival_gap: From the organized blocs' perspective, the floor is a natural law — an irreducible feature of any large-scale democratic system. From the unorganized publics' perspective, the same structure operates as systematic exclusion. From the political scientists' perspective, the floor is an empirical regularity whose naturalness is contested. The engine computes these divergences from the structural data — the authored claim (Mountain) does not adjudicate them.
commentary.mandatrophy_analysis: The constraint solves a real coordination problem (warrantability in policy exchange) but the solution systematically advantages some actors over others. This is the classic Tangled Rope structure — genuine coordination function coupled to asymmetric extraction. However, the constraint presents as a natural law (Mountain) because the coordination problem is real and the floor appears to emerge from transaction cost economics. The false summit machinery evaluates whether the Mountain claim is warranted or whether the beneficiary structure indicates a constructed constraint dressed as natural law. The measurement series showing extraction accumulation over time as technology has reduced underlying transaction costs supports the false summit hypothesis.

omegas.question: Is the organization floor an irreducible property of large-scale democratic systems, or is it a constructed feature of specific institutional arrangements that could be substantially lowered by institutional reform?
omegas.resolution_mechanism: Natural experiments from jurisdictions that have implemented direct democracy mechanisms, sortition, or alternative voting systems. If the organization threshold is substantially lower in those systems, the floor is institutional rather than natural.
omegas.impact: If the floor is institutional, the Mountain claim is false and the constraint should reclassify as Tangled Rope (coordination function coupled to asymmetric extraction maintained by institutional features). If the floor is natural, the Mountain claim is warranted despite the beneficiary structure.
omegas.description: Whether the organization floor is a natural law or an institutional artifact.

omegas.question: How much of the floor's current height is explained by irreducible transaction costs, and how much is explained by organized interests' active defense of institutional features that maintain the floor?
omegas.resolution_mechanism: Decomposition analysis comparing the floor's height in the pre-digital era (when transaction costs were genuinely high) to its current height (when communication technology has reduced many transaction costs). If the floor has not fallen proportionally to the transaction cost reduction, the gap is institutional defense.
omegas.impact: A large gap would establish that organized interests are actively maintaining a floor higher than transaction costs require, supporting reclassification from Mountain to Tangled Rope. A small gap would support the natural law framing.
omegas.description: Whether the floor's current height tracks transaction costs or institutional defense.

omegas.question: Is the systematic advantage organized interests capture from the floor an efficiency property (they are the only actors who can credibly commit, so they should get policy influence) or a distributional pathology (they capture rents beyond what their commitment capacity warrants)?
omegas.resolution_mechanism: Welfare analysis comparing policy outcomes in systems with high organization floors to systems with lower floors. If lower-floor systems produce comparable or better welfare outcomes, the advantage is distributional pathology rather than efficiency.
omegas.impact: If the advantage is efficiency, the extraction is the price of the coordination function and the Mountain claim is warranted. If it is distributional pathology, the extraction exceeds coordination cost and the constraint should reclassify.
omegas.description: Whether organized interests' advantage is efficiency or rent extraction.

network.dual_formulation_note: The organization floor is one constraint in a family of democratic institutional features that interact to determine whose preferences are tradable in policy markets. Legislative procedure rules, geographic representation systems, and voting mechanisms all affect the floor's height. This story focuses on the floor itself as the threshold phenomenon; the institutional features that maintain it are separate constraints linked via network edges.
